discussion_comments.comment_body: Probably an existing type-issue but according to types `InitializationHandler` can only have a `BlockedChunk` so why do we need to check status here at runtime?

This is a real runtime condition. `BlockedChunk` is the chunk's type when the handler recorded it, but the object is mutated in place: it can have been errored by `rejectReference` (any of the handler's references failing) or completed by a cyclic reference during the drain loop before the last `deps--` arrives here. Both inline blocks this replaces had the same check on `main`. I made it explicit with the `SomeChunk` cast that
`wakeChunkIfInitialized` uses, and a comment.

Nice idea, that made the cleanup much simpler. It also automatically handles the cancelled stream case.

We should make search asynchronous.

When the search input is updated, we should update it synchronously, e.g. just calling `setSearchTextState(text)`. But finding matches should be done in a transition, because otherwise it may block the update that will change the input text.

Keep controlled input updates sync, and put other updates in a transition.

Done. The controlled input now updates synchronously (setSearchTextState(text)), and the match computation is deferred: searchResults is derived from useDeferredValue(searchText), so the tree walk runs at transition priority and never blocks the input update. I went with useDeferredValue rather than startTransition since searchResults is a derived value — it's the transition-priority tool for derived data, and it keeps results scoped to the current commit for free (the memo re-derives on commit change). Selecting the current match now reacts to the deferred results.

discussion_comments.comment_body: The tuple is only for one specific usage. The array is really about ensuring that an array is written atomically. So either we explain the generic use case (array), or type and handle only tuples. We should probably really just handle a tuple. I don't know what happens if we later start pushing actual arrays that bypass backpressure.

Due to only using the last value to decide if we continue writing, there's an implicit assumption that `writeChunkAndReturn` wouldn't just flip from `false` to `true`.

The Node.js implementation is explicit https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/cafd63bcf755ed163cfe07f3c685311233da5a9f/packages/react-server/src/ReactServerStreamConfigNode.js#L172. 

Not sure though if we need to be consistent.
It's fine if it flips from `false` to `true`. That just means backpressure is relieved and we can continue writing more chunks.
